items.title: 4-figure grid references give 1 km precision; 6-figure give 100 m
items.claim: What precision do OS grid references provide?

options.text: 4-figure references identify a 1 km × 1 km square; 6-figure references identify a 100 m × 100 m square; 8-figure references give 10 m precision — read 'eastings before northings', 'along the corridor, up the stairs'
References are accurate to 1 metre regardless

items.reveal:
OS uses a National Grid: read eastings (horizontal) first, then northings (vertical). Grid letters (NY, SE, etc.) identify 100 km squares.

A full reference combines letters with numerical eastings/northings — e.g. SE 543 367 for 100 m precision. The National Grid covers Great Britain; Northern Ireland uses the Irish Grid; the Channel Islands use UTM.

GPS coordinates (latitude/longitude or UTM) are international alternatives. Reporting accident or weather locations with inconsistent precision causes real navigation failures, including in search-and-rescue.
items.why: Map references are not arbitrary precision. Search and rescue, weather reporting and fieldwork all depend on consistent referencing — and the difference between 4 and 6 figures is the difference between 'somewhere in this 1 km square' and 'within a tennis court'.

items.title: Yellowstone has erupted as a supervolcano roughly every 600,000 years
items.claim: What is the recurrence interval of major Yellowstone caldera eruptions?

options.text: Every 10,000 years — overdue many times over
The last three major caldera-forming eruptions were around 2.1 million, 1.3 million and 631,000 years ago — an average interval of around 725,000 years, with no implied 'due date'
Every century — but eruptions have been small
Yellowstone has never been a supervolcano

items.reveal:
USGS Yellowstone Volcano Observatory data: Huckleberry Ridge (2.1 Ma), Mesa Falls (1.3 Ma), Lava Creek (631 ka). The last lava flow was 70,000 years ago. The current scientific consensus is that Yellowstone shows no signs of an imminent eruption.

Toba (Sumatra, around 74,000 years ago) ejected around 2,800 km³ of material — the largest eruption in the last 25 million years. The Yellowstone Lava Creek eruption ejected around 1,000 km³.

A VEI 8 eruption today would devastate North America with ashfall and disrupt global climate for years.
items.why: 'Overdue' supervolcano narratives misuse averages. Three datapoints do not establish a periodic schedule — and absent any geophysical signal of imminent eruption, the right answer is 'we don't know when, but not soon'.

items.title: Cities are typically 2-5 °C warmer than surrounding countryside
items.claim: What is the urban heat island effect?

options.text: A myth — cities are no warmer than rural areas

Cities are typically 2-5 °C warmer than surrounding rural areas (up to 10 °C at night in extremes) due to dark surfaces (low albedo), reduced evapotranspiration, anthropogenic heat and reduced sky view
Cities are colder than countryside due to shade
Only New York shows the effect

items.reveal:
Causes: low-albedo asphalt and concrete absorb solar radiation; reduced vegetation cuts evaporative cooling; tall buildings trap re-emitted infrared (sky-view factor); waste heat from vehicles, buildings and air conditioning; thermal mass releases heat at night.

London during the August 2003 heatwave was around 4-9 °C warmer than surrounding countryside at night; UHI contributed to the death toll (around 2,000 excess deaths in the UK). Paris 2003 saw around 15,000 excess deaths.

Mitigation: green roofs, urban trees (Singapore, Melbourne), light-coloured surfaces (Los Angeles cool roofs), water features, ventilation corridors in city planning.
items.why: Urban climate is human-made microclimate. Climate change interacts with UHI to make heatwaves more dangerous in cities — a fast-rising public health hazard.
